Problem: Existing knowledge graphs (KGs) adopted in recommender systems are limited, with low usability, significantly sparse, and lack facts due to expensive supervision, leading to missing entities or relations and ignored user preferences.
Context: Knowledge bases, particularly knowledge graphs, provide rich semantic information to enhance recommender system performance. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive power in storing factual information and commonsense knowledge, presenting an opportunity to construct more comprehensive KGs.
Solution: Leverage LLMs' capabilities to solve knowledge graph completion (predicting missing facts) and knowledge graph construction (entity discovery, coreference resolution, relation extraction, end-to-end KG building from raw text). LLMs can also enable knowledge distillation to construct KGs.
Result: Recommender systems benefit from a more extensive and up-to-date knowledge base. Missing factual information is completed, relations between entities are extracted for better recommenders, and cross-domain information from LLMs enables cross-domain recommendations, ultimately enhancing recommendation accuracy, relevance, and personalization.
Related Patterns: Knowledge Graph Completion, Knowledge Graph Construction, Knowledge Distillation
Uses: Enhancing CTR prediction models, enriching item information, determining complementary relationships in entity pairs for industrial recommenders.
Thinking: This pattern describes how LLMs are used to directly address a core AI problem in knowledge representation and management for other AI systems (recommender systems), leveraging LLMs' unique knowledge storage and reasoning capabilities to build and complete structured knowledge.

Problem: Content features in content-based recommendation can be sparse, and traditional content interpreters (statistical models, neural networks) struggle to capture complex semantic information effectively, limiting the full exploitation of content features. There's also a misalignment of goals between general-purpose language models and specific recommendation objectives, and high online inference latency.
Context: Content-based recommenders rely on item attributes for understanding properties and matching user preferences. Powerful pretrained language models (PLMs/LLMs) like BERT and GPT have shown exceptional performance in NLP tasks, capturing deep semantic representations and world knowledge.
Solution: Employ powerful pretrained language models as content interpreters. This involves fine-tuning PLMs for recommendation tasks (e.g., masked opinion token prediction, opinion rating prediction), reducing online inference latency through knowledge distillation and model optimization, and leveraging LLMs' emergent abilities in reasoning and generalization (e.g., instruction tuning for sequential recommendation, few-shot learning, cross-domain generalization).
Result: Enhanced understanding and interpretation of textual content, leading to improved recommendations. Alleviation of cold-start problems and facilitation of cross-domain recommendations. Better capture of deep semantic representations, world knowledge, and user preferences, enabling effective handling of diverse recommendation tasks.
Related Patterns: Fine-tuning, Knowledge Distillation, Instruction Tuning, Zero-shot Learning, Few-shot Learning
Uses: News recommendation, tag recommendation, tweet representations, code example recommendation, zero-shot recommendation, cross-domain sequential recommendation, rating prediction, item recommendation, personalized search.
Thinking: This pattern focuses on using LLMs as a sophisticated AI component to process and understand content (textual features) for other AI systems (recommender systems), overcoming limitations of prior AI models in semantic understanding and generalization for this specific task.

Problem: Most recommender systems are black boxes, diminishing user trust due to inscrutable inner workings. Traditional explanation methods (template-based, early natural language generation) are inflexible, lack diversity, coherence, and generalizability, and are tightly coupled with specific recommendation models.
Context: Users desire comprehensible justifications for recommendations to improve trust, transparency, persuasiveness, and error identification. LLMs possess remarkable generative abilities in language tasks, extensive training data, and unique in-context learning capabilities.
Solution: Leverage LLMs' generative ability and in-context learning (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought prompting) to craft customized, precise, natural, and adaptable explanations. LLMs can harness human language, gather real-time user feedback, and provide model-agnostic interpretations, distinguishing them from traditional methods tied to specific algorithms.
Result: Improved transparency, persuasiveness, and reliability of recommender systems. More diverse, coherent, and personalized explanations that adapt to user preferences. A versatile and scalable interpretational framework with broader applicability, independent of the underlying recommendation model's architecture.
Related Patterns: In-context Learning, Zero-shot Prompting, Few-shot Prompting, Chain-of-Thought Prompting, Natural Language Generation
Uses: Explainable visualization recommendation, general recommendation model interpretability.
Thinking: This pattern directly addresses the AI-specific problem of interpretability and explainability for black-box AI models (recommender systems) by leveraging the unique generative and reasoning capabilities of LLMs to produce human-understandable justifications.

Problem: Traditional recommender systems require explicit training or tuning for new cases, and there's a need for systems that can provide recommendations without extensive prior training, especially in open-domain scenarios or for cold-start situations. While LLMs show promise, a substantial performance gap still exists compared to fine-tuned, task-specific models.
Context: LLMs exhibit emergent reasoning abilities and in-context learning, allowing them to generate outputs based on natural language instructions and a few demonstrations (shots) without explicit training or tuning. They possess significant commonsense knowledge from extensive open-domain training.
Solution: Employ LLMs directly for recommendation tasks (e.g., rating prediction, ranking prediction) using in-context learning (zero-shot or few-shot prompting). For ranking tasks, a candidate generation module may be integrated. Utilize Chain-of-Thought prompting strategies to enable LLMs to perform step-by-step reasoning, breaking down complex recommendation tasks into intermediate steps.
Result: Ability to provide recommendations on new cases without explicit tuning. Improved performance in few-shot scenarios compared to zero-shot. Enhanced recommendation performance through multi-step reasoning, capturing user preferences, filtering items, and reranking.
Related Patterns: In-context Learning, Zero-shot Learning, Few-shot Learning, Chain-of-Thought Prompting
Uses: Rating prediction, ranking prediction, sequential recommendation, direct recommendation, explanation generation, review summarization.
Thinking: This pattern describes using LLMs' inherent reasoning and in-context learning abilities directly for the core AI task of recommendation, representing a paradigm shift in how recommendations are generated without traditional model training.

Problem: Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) in recommender systems involves costly manual setup with trials and errors. The search space for optimal configurations (embedding size, features, interactions, model architecture) is considerably complex, diverse, and lacks a strong foundation of domain-specific knowledge.
Context: LLMs have excellent memorization and reasoning capabilities that can be applied to automated learning. AutoML aims to eliminate manual effort by automating the search for optimal AI model components or configurations.
Solution: Integrate LLMs into AutoML processes for recommender systems to guide the automated selection of model architectures or components. This can involve using LLMs' generative capability to formulate network architectures (GPTNAS), employing LLMs as black-box agents to generate better-performing architectures based on previous trials (GENIUS), or integrating LLMs into hybrid search strategies (e.g., genetic algorithms) where LLMs act as mutation and crossover operators (LLMatic, EvoPrompting).
Result: Reduced manual effort and search space in AutoML for recommender systems. Generation of reasonable or better-performing architectures. Improved efficiency and interpretability in complex search tasks by leveraging LLMs' reasoning to guide the search process.
Related Patterns: AutoML, Neural Architecture Search (NAS), Genetic Algorithms (LLM-augmented)
Uses: Embedding size search, feature selection, feature interaction search, model architecture search in recommender systems.
Thinking: This pattern uses an AI (LLM) to assist in the design, optimization, and automation of *other* AI models or components within recommender systems, which is a meta-AI design pattern for improving AI development itself.

Problem: Building enterprise-level Conversational Recommender Systems (CRS) faces significant challenges: LLMs often lack awareness of private domain data, and they have memory and comprehension limitations in long conversations due to input token constraints, leading to the omission of valuable historical information.
Context: Conversational recommender systems aim to uncover user interests through dialogue for personalized recommendations. LLMs possess inherent conversational capabilities due to extensive open-domain training and instruction tuning, making them suitable for CRSs.
Solution: Address private domain data challenges through fine-tuning LLMs with domain-specific dialogue data (potentially generated by user simulators) or via tool learning, where traditional recommendation models are treated as tools for LLMs. Address long conversation memory limitations by incorporating memory modules (e.g., MemPrompt) or user profile modules (e.g., RecLLM) to store and retrieve relevant user facts, or by summarizing/compressing dialogue history.
Result: Enhanced ability of CRSs to understand user intents, adapt recommendations, and provide personalized experiences in private domains. Improved long-term memory and comprehension in multi-turn dialogues, maintaining context and accuracy of recommendations.
Related Patterns: Fine-tuning, Tool Learning, User Simulators, Prompt Engineering (Chain of Thought, ToT, Plan-and-Solve, ReAct), Memory-Augmented LLMs
Uses: Conversational search, personalized assistance, enterprise-level conversational recommender systems.
Thinking: This pattern describes how LLMs are specifically engineered and integrated to act as the core AI component of a conversational system, addressing challenges unique to AI-driven dialogue management, domain adaptation, and context retention.

Problem: Foundational models (LLMs) have powerful natural language processing capabilities but may lack specific knowledge, computational abilities, or real-world interaction capabilities required for complex tasks beyond their inherent understanding.
Context: Tool learning is an emerging research field combining specialized tools with foundational models. LLMs can break down complex tasks into subtasks and convert them into executable instructions, while specialized tools can provide external knowledge, computational power, or specific functionalities.
Solution: LLMs act as controllers to select, manage, and aggregate results from various existing AI models or specialized tools (e.g., search engines, calculators, recommendation engines, databases). This involves 'Tool-augmented learning' (tools assist LLMs) and 'Tool-oriented learning' (LLMs learn to use tools effectively). Some advanced approaches even enable LLMs to directly generate tools.
Result: LLMs gain access to knowledge beyond their own understanding, perform complex computations, interact with external systems, and address complex problems more accurately and efficiently, leading to flexible decision-making and improved generalization capabilities.
Related Patterns: Tool-augmented Learning, Tool-oriented Learning, Self-generation of Tools, ReAct, Toolformer
Uses: General complex task solving, visual tasks, mathematical reasoning, robotic tasks, knowledge-intensive language tasks.
Thinking: This is a meta-AI design pattern where an LLM acts as an intelligent orchestrator for a collection of other AI models or specialized computational tools, extending its own AI capabilities by intelligently delegating subtasks and integrating results.

Problem: Despite their impressive capabilities, LLMs struggle with memorizing specific knowledge in private and specialized domains, controlling their behavior within a specific domain, and handling the temporal generalization problem as external knowledge evolves.
Context: LLMs demonstrate impressive abilities in understanding user intent from dialogues and communicating fluently in natural language, making them appealing choices as recommendation agents.
Solution: Augment LLMs with various specialized tools to enhance their effectiveness as recommendation agents. This includes integrating search engines to provide external knowledge and reduce hallucinations, equipping LLMs with recommendation engines (e.g., retrieve and rerank stages) to ground recommendations on item corpora, and utilizing databases (vector databases for new items, user profile modules for enduring user facts) to supplement domain-specific and personalized information.
Result: LLMs can offer recommendations grounded on specific item corpora, handle cold-start problems for new items, alleviate the temporal generalization problem, and provide more authentic and personalized information by leveraging external, up-to-date knowledge.
Related Patterns: LLM-based Tool Orchestration, Search Engine Integration, Recommendation Engine Integration, Database Integration
Uses: Personalized recommendations, cold-start problem alleviation, factual information provision in conversational recommender systems.
Thinking: This pattern is a specific application of 'LLM-based Tool Orchestration' tailored for personalization. It describes how an LLM acts as an intelligent recommendation agent by strategically leveraging other AI/data tools to overcome its inherent limitations in domain-specific knowledge and real-time data access.

Problem: Traditional recommender systems only suggest existing items. There's a growing need for customized, appealing content generated to match users' specific interests and preferences, especially in online advertising, where earlier methods (templates, data-driven RL) often fail to fully meet user interests or capture explicit preferences.
Context: The advancements in AI Generated Content (AIGC) techniques (GANs, VAEs, diffusion models, transformers) and the emergence of large language models (ChatGPT, DALL-E 2, Codex) enable the creation of high-quality digital content from instructions, by extracting human intention and generating content based on knowledge.
Solution: Integrate LLMs and AIGC techniques to create personalized content. This involves leveraging LLMs for better reasoning of user personalized intent and interest (enhancing few-shot prompting), applying Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to fine-tune models for better intent capture, utilizing LLMs' powerful generative abilities and cross-modal knowledge bases for realistic content creation, and designing feedback loops for multiple rounds of conversion to capture explicit user preferences.
Result: More appealing, customized content (visual, semantic, text ads, ad banners, thumbnails, videos) that precisely matches user interests and preferences. Improved reasoning of user intent, better capture of explicit preferences, realistic content generation, and significant alleviation of the sparse feedback problem in content creation.
Related Patterns: AIGC, RLHF, Multimodal Generation, Few-shot Prompting
Uses: Online advertising (ad title and description generation, ad banners, thumbnails, videos), chatbots for personalized product recommendations, automated responses, FAQs, and personalized assistance in customer service.
Thinking: This pattern describes using LLMs as generative AI models to *create* new, personalized content, moving beyond traditional recommendation of existing items. It's a direct application of generative AI for personalization, leveraging LLMs' unique creative and understanding capabilities.

Problem: Language Model (LM) agents struggle to reliably interact with complex digital environments (e.g., Linux shell) using interfaces designed for humans. These human-centric interfaces are often too granular, verbose, lack specific feedback, or are visually oriented, which LMs cannot process effectively. This leads to poor performance, inefficiency, and an inability for LMs to autonomously solve complex tasks.
Context: Developing LM agents to perform complex tasks in digital environments (e.g., software engineering, web navigation, computer control) where they act as a new category of end-user with distinct needs and abilities compared to humans.
Solution: Introduce an abstraction layer, the Agent-Computer Interface (ACI), between the LM agent and the computer. This interface is specifically designed for LMs, offering a tailored set of simple, efficient actions, providing concise and informative feedback, and incorporating guardrails to prevent common mistakes. It shapes actions, their documentation, and environment feedback to complement an LM's limitations and abilities.
Result: Substantially enhances the LM agent's ability to interact with computer environments, leading to significantly improved performance, reliability, and efficiency on complex tasks (e.g., state-of-the-art on SWEbench and HumanEvalFix). It unifies tool use, prompting techniques, and code execution within a single framework.
Related Patterns: LM-Friendly Commands, Informative & Concise Feedback, Guardrails for Agents, Context Management for Agents.
Uses: Automating software engineering tasks, general digital environment interaction for LM agents, any scenario where LMs need to interact with software applications.
Thinking: This is the core, overarching AI design pattern explicitly introduced and justified in the text. It defines a new type of interface specifically for AI agents, acknowledging their unique cognitive and processing characteristics (e.g., lack of visual understanding, token-based processing).

Problem: Traditional command-line tools (e.g., Bash commands) often have complex syntax, numerous options, and verbose documentation. This complexity makes them difficult for LM agents to parse, understand, and use reliably, leading to frequent errors, inefficient action composition, and increased cognitive load (in terms of token processing).
Context: Designing the action space within an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) for LM agents that need to perform operations like file manipulation, search, and navigation in a digital environment. The goal is to enable efficient and reliable action-taking.
Solution: Design commands to be simple, compact, and efficient. This involves: 1. Simplicity: Commands should have few options and concise documentation, reducing the need for extensive demonstrations or fine-tuning. 2. Efficiency: Important operations (e.g., multi-line file editing, specific file navigation) should be consolidated into as few actions as possible, allowing the agent to make meaningful progress in a single step rather than composing many simple actions.
Result: Commands become easier for LM agents to use, reducing errors and the cognitive burden of complex syntax. Agents can achieve higher-order operations more efficiently, making meaningful progress towards goals in fewer turns and conserving context window space.
Related Patterns: Agent-Computer Interface (ACI), Informative & Concise Feedback.
Uses: Defining the action set for LM agents interacting with file systems, code editors, search tools, or any application requiring command execution.
Thinking: This pattern directly addresses the cognitive limitations of LMs (e.g., difficulty with complex instructions, preference for simplicity) and their processing constraints (e.g., token cost of verbose documentation), making it specific to AI design.

Problem: Raw or verbose environment feedback (e.g., full `cat` output, unparsed `grep` results, silent command success) can be overwhelming, uninformative, or contain too much irrelevant detail for LM agents. LMs incur fixed costs for all content in their context window, and distracting or verbose information can harm performance and exhaust the context window prematurely.
Context: Providing environment observations back to an LM agent within an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) after it executes an action. The agent needs to understand the current state and the effects of its actions to plan the next step effectively.
Solution: Design feedback mechanisms to be both informative and concise. This includes: 1. Substantive Information: Provide meaningful details about the current environment state and the direct effects of the agent's actions (e.g., updated file content after an edit, line numbers in a file viewer). 2. Conciseness: Omit unnecessary details. For example, search results are capped (e.g., 50 matches), file viewer shows a limited window (e.g., 100 lines) with context indicators, and silent successful commands receive explicit 'success, no output' messages.
Result: Enables the LM agent to better understand the application's state and the impact of its actions, facilitating more accurate planning and decision-making. Reduces context window bloat, allowing for more interaction turns and preventing the agent from being 'lost in the middle' or acting on outdated information.
Related Patterns: Agent-Computer Interface (ACI), Context Management for Agents.
Uses: Any interactive LM agent system where environment observations are critical for iterative decision-making, particularly in tasks involving code inspection, search, and execution.
Thinking: This pattern is specifically tailored to the context window limitations and information processing characteristics of LMs, recognizing that they process all tokens and can be distracted by irrelevant information, unlike humans who can filter visually.

Problem: LM agents, like human users, can introduce errors (e.g., syntax errors, logical inconsistencies) when performing actions, especially in complex domains like code editing. These errors can propagate, lead to cascading failures, and make it difficult for the agent to recognize and recover, significantly hampering performance and wasting computational resources.
Context: Designing the action execution and feedback loop within an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) for LM agents, particularly in tasks where agent actions can modify the environment in ways that introduce errors (e.g., code generation and editing).
Solution: Implement automated validation and error mitigation mechanisms (guardrails) that intervene when an agent's action would lead to a detectable error. For example, integrate a code linter into the file editor that checks for syntax errors. If an error is detected: 1. The invalid action is discarded (e.g., the edit is reverted). 2. The agent receives specific, informative feedback about the error (e.g., linter error messages, snippet of proposed change vs. original code). 3. The agent is prompted to correct its action and try again.
Result: Prevents the propagation of errors, hastens the agent's recovery from mistakes, and significantly improves overall task performance by ensuring that only valid or non-error-introducing changes are applied to the environment.
Related Patterns: Agent-Computer Interface (ACI), Informative & Concise Feedback.
Uses: Code editing, configuration updates, or any agent action that modifies a structured environment where automated validation rules can be applied to prevent common errors.
Thinking: This pattern addresses a specific failure mode of LMs (introducing errors and struggling to recover) by providing an automated, AI-centric error handling and recovery mechanism within the interface, leveraging computational checks to guide the LM.

Problem: In multi-turn interactions, the full history of commands, observations, and error messages can quickly exceed the fixed context window size of Language Models. This leads to 'lost in the middle' phenomena, where LMs struggle to attend to relevant information, or to outdated information being presented, which degrades performance and limits the number of interaction turns possible.
Context: Maintaining and presenting the interaction history to an LM agent within an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) during long-running, iterative tasks in digital environments.
Solution: Implement strategies to keep the agent's context concise and relevant. Key techniques include: 1. History Processors: Collapse older observations (e.g., all but the last 5) into single-line placeholders, preserving the interaction structure but removing verbose content. 2. Error Message Filtering: Omit repeated error messages, showing only the first instance to avoid redundancy. 3. Clarity for Silent Actions: Provide explicit messages for commands that run successfully but produce no output (e.g., 'Your command ran successfully and did not produce any output') to prevent agent confusion. 4. Prompting: Provide initial instructions, documentation, and demonstrations to set up the context effectively.
Result: Optimizes the use of the LM's context window, allowing for more interaction cycles and preventing performance degradation due to excessive or irrelevant information. It ensures the agent has access to essential plan and action history without being overwhelmed by outdated or redundant details.
Related Patterns: Agent-Computer Interface (ACI), Informative & Concise Feedback.
Uses: Any multi-turn LM agent system where the length of interaction history is a critical factor for performance and resource management (e.g., token cost).
Thinking: This pattern is fundamentally about managing the computational and cognitive resources of an LM (specifically its context window and attention mechanisms) to ensure effective long-term interaction, making it a core AI design pattern.

Problem: Directly using Large Language Models (LLMs) for planning leads to limited correctness, strong reliance on online feedback, and inefficiency in utilizing human feedback. Manually constructing explicit symbolic world models (e.g., PDDL) is complex and requires specialized expertise, hindering broader adoption.
Context: An AI agent needs to perform sequential decision-making (planning) tasks. Pretrained LLMs are available, possessing extensive common-world knowledge and natural language understanding capabilities, but lack robust symbolic reasoning and combinatorial search abilities. An explicit, sound symbolic world model is desired for reliable planning.
Solution: Leverage pretrained LLMs to construct explicit symbolic world models (e.g., PDDL domain models). This involves prompting the LLM with detailed instructions, examples, domain context, natural language descriptions of actions, and a dynamically updated list of predicates. The LLM acts as a PDDL constructor, utilizing its common-world knowledge for knowledge acquisition (proposing preconditions/effects) and its natural language parsing ability to precisely represent explicit constraints. The process can be iterative, generating models action-by-action and refining predicates.
Result: High-quality, explicit symbolic world models (e.g., PDDL) are generated, enabling the use of sound domain-independent planners. This reduces the initial human involvement in model creation and allows LLMs to focus on tasks they are more proficient in (modeling causal dependencies) rather than combinatorial search.
Related Patterns: Learning/Acquiring Symbolic Domain Models, LLM as Knowledge Base, Natural Language to Formal Specification.
Uses: Initial setup of AI agents, expanding the set of actions for an agent, constructing models for specialized domains, providing a foundation for reliable planning.
Thinking: This pattern describes how an LLM, an AI component, is used to *create* another AI component (a symbolic world model) that is crucial for AI planning. It addresses a specific AI problem (LLM planning limitations) with an AI-centric solution (LLM as a model constructor).

Pattern Name: LLM-Mediated Corrective Feedback Loop for Symbolic Models
Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) may not generate fully functional or error-free symbolic models initially. Correcting these models directly requires expertise in the symbolic language (e.g., PDDL), which many end-users lack. Repeatedly providing the same feedback for similar errors can lead to user frustration.
Context: A symbolic world model (e.g., PDDL) has been generated, potentially by an LLM, and requires validation and correction. Feedback sources, such as PDDL validators (for syntax errors) or human domain experts (for factual errors), provide corrective feedback, often in natural language.
Solution: Employ an LLM as an intelligent interface or middle layer between the underlying symbolic model and the feedback sources. The LLM translates the symbolic representation (PDDL) into natural language for user inspection. It then processes natural language corrective feedback (from humans or translated validator messages) and incorporates it back into the symbolic model. This conceals the complexity of the symbolic language from non-expert users. The correction process involves replaying and continuing the model construction dialogue.
Result: Error-free and functional symbolic world models are achieved. The process reduces the cognitive burden on users, enables seamless inclusion of feedback, and prevents repeated errors by archiving corrections directly into the model.
Related Patterns: Human-in-the-Loop AI, Interactive Model Acquisition, LLM as Interface, Self-Correction (when feedback is internal).
Uses: Refining LLM-generated PDDL models, ensuring the correctness and usability of symbolic world models, making symbolic model acquisition accessible to non-experts.
Thinking: This pattern uses an LLM to facilitate the *correction and refinement* of an AI's internal representation (the symbolic model). It's AI-specific because it leverages the LLM's natural language understanding and generation to bridge the gap between human feedback and a formal AI model, directly improving the quality of an AI system's knowledge.

Problem: Large Language Models (LLMs) alone lack sufficient reasoning and planning capabilities to reliably generate correct and executable plans, especially for complex tasks or those requiring long-term dependencies. However, they excel at understanding natural language instructions.
Context: An explicit, sound symbolic world model (e.g., PDDL) has been acquired (potentially using LLM-Assisted Symbolic World Model Construction). A user provides high-level instructions or tasks in natural language. The goal is to generate a reliable and correct plan.
Solution: Utilize an LLM primarily for its natural language understanding capabilities to translate user instructions into symbolic goal specifications (e.g., PDDL goals). These symbolic goals, along with the LLM-acquired symbolic world model, are then passed to a standard, domain-independent classical planner (e.g., Fast Downward). The classical planner performs the combinatorial search to find a satisficing or optimal sequence of actions.
Result: Reliably generated, correct, and executable plans with high success rates, leveraging the correctness guarantees and robust search capabilities of classical planners. This approach effectively combines the LLM's strength in natural language interpretation with the symbolic planner's strength in logical reasoning and search.
Related Patterns: LLM as Tool User, Natural Language to Formal Specification, Symbolic Planning.
Uses: Generating reliable plans for complex tasks in various domains (e.g., household robotics, logistics), where plan correctness is paramount.
Thinking: This is an AI design pattern because it describes a specific architecture for combining two distinct AI paradigms (LLMs for NL understanding, symbolic planners for search) to solve an AI problem (reliable planning). The LLM acts as a crucial pre-processor for the symbolic planner.

Pattern Name: Hybrid LLM-Symbolic Planning (LLM Planner with Symbolic Validation)
Problem: While Large Language Model (LLM) planners can incorporate implicit user constraints and offer flexibility, they are prone to errors, overlook preconditions, and struggle with plan correctness and executability. Relying on faithful simulators or extensive manual inspection for feedback is costly or impractical.
Context: An LLM is intended to be the primary planner, potentially leveraging its ability to handle implicit constraints or common-sense reasoning. A symbolic world model (e.g., PDDL) is available and can serve as an inexpensive, high-level simulator or human proxy for plan validation.
Solution: An LLM planner (e.g., using ReAct) generates a plan. This plan, along with the symbolic goal specifications, initial states, and the LLM-acquired symbolic domain model, is passed to a plan validation system (e.g., VAL). The validation system checks for unmet preconditions or goal conditions. The validation results, which are typically symbolic, are then translated into natural language (by an LLM) and provided as corrective feedback to the LLM planner. The LLM planner iteratively refines its plan through reprompting based on this feedback.
Result: Improved plan correctness and executability compared to vanilla LLM planners. This approach reduces reliance on expensive simulators and allows the LLM planner to benefit from the logical consistency checks of a symbolic model, while still potentially incorporating implicit user constraints.
Related Patterns: Corrective Reprompting, LLM as Plan Critic, Human-in-the-Loop (simulated), ReAct.
Uses: Enhancing the reliability of LLM-generated plans, especially in commonsense domains where LLMs might capture subtle user preferences, while still ensuring basic logical correctness.
Thinking: This pattern describes an AI system where an LLM (as a planner) is augmented by another AI component (a symbolic model used for validation) in a feedback loop. The LLM's output is critiqued by a formal system, and the LLM uses that critique to improve, making it a clear AI design pattern for robust AI agent behavior.

Problem: Foundation models need to accurately interpret user goals from natural language, which can be vague, imprecise, or polysemous, requiring reliance on contextual cues and background knowledge.
Context: A foundation model (controller) receives natural language instructions from a user in a tool-learning scenario, where the model needs to perform tasks by manipulating tools.
Solution: Leverage foundation models' strong language understanding capabilities, enhanced by instruction tuning. Actively interact with users to clarify any ambiguity (e.g., asking for clarifications). Adapt to diverse expressions of intent, potentially through personalized tool learning.
Result: Models can provide more personalized and precise responses, effectively bridging the gap between user intent and the available tool set, which is a prerequisite for connecting the controller, user, and tool set.
Related Patterns: Personalized Tool Learning, Instruction Tuning, Few-shot Learning, Zero-shot Learning.
Uses: Any AI system or agent that interacts with users via natural language to perform tasks, especially those involving external tools or complex decision-making.
Thinking: This pattern describes how an AI model comprehends human language to infer goals, a core AI capability. It leverages AI-specific techniques like instruction tuning and addresses challenges unique to natural language processing by AI.

Problem: Foundation models need to comprehend the functionalities and usage of various tools to use them proficiently, often from accompanying manuals or tutorials.
Context: A foundation model (controller) is presented with a tool set, where each tool typically has an API, description, or usage examples. The model needs to learn how to interact with these tools.
Solution: Utilize foundation models' strong few-shot and zero-shot learning capabilities through suitable task-specific prompts. This can involve: 1) **Zero-shot prompting:** Describing API functionalities, input/output formats, and parameters. 2) **Few-shot prompting:** Providing concrete tool-use demonstrations to the model.
Result: Models can unravel tool functionalities and comprehend how to use them with minimal human effort. Prompts can be easily adjusted to accommodate changes or upgrades to tools, allowing flexible adaptation of model behaviors.
Related Patterns: Few-shot Learning, Zero-shot Learning, Prompt Engineering, In-context Learning.
Uses: Integrating new or existing tools into a foundation model's capabilities, enabling rapid adaptation to diverse tool sets without extensive re-training.
Thinking: This pattern details an AI-specific method (prompting, few-shot/zero-shot learning) for an AI model to acquire knowledge about external components (tools), which is distinct from traditional software integration.

Problem: User queries often imply complex tasks that need to be divided into multiple subtasks with proper sequencing, necessitating a process of reasoning to generate an executable plan for tool execution.
Context: A foundation model (controller) receives a complex user instruction that cannot be fulfilled by a single tool call or simple action. The model needs to orchestrate multiple tools or actions.
Solution: Leverage the emergent reasoning capabilities of scaled-up foundation models. These models can decompose high-level tasks into semantically plausible subplans, determine which tool to call for each subproblem, and generate intermediate reasoning traces (e.g., Chain of Thought prompting).
Result: Models can effectively decompose complex problems and generate multi-step plans for tool use, significantly enhancing their performance on complex problem-solving tasks.
Related Patterns: Introspective Reasoning, Extrospective Reasoning, Chain of Thought Prompting, Multi-step Multi-tool Scenario.
Uses: Any AI agent needing to solve multi-step problems by orchestrating multiple actions or tools, especially in complex interactive environments.
Thinking: This pattern describes how AI models perform complex cognitive tasks like planning and reasoning, which are central to AI's ability to solve problems beyond simple pattern recognition. It highlights emergent abilities of large models.

Problem: Generating a multi-step plan for tool use without real-time environmental feedback, where the entire plan must be formulated upfront.
Context: A foundation model needs to generate a complete sequence of tool actions or programs for a task, without direct interaction with the environment during the planning phase. The environment is 'invisible' to the controller during this process.
Solution: Models directly generate static, multi-step plans or executable programs (e.g., Python code for intermediate reasoning steps in Program-Aided Language Models (PAL), or programs for embodied agents in ProgPrompt/Code as Policies) based on their internal knowledge and reasoning capabilities.
Result: Enables models to act as 'programmers' generating detailed, executable plans and anticipating possible anomalies. Achieves significant improvements in arithmetic, symbolic, and algorithmic reasoning. However, plans may be unrealistic if not sufficiently grounded.
Related Patterns: Program-Aided Language Models (PAL), Model-as-Programmer, ProgPrompt, Code as Policies.
Uses: Tasks where the environment is predictable or a full plan can be generated offline, or where the model needs to act as a code generator for tool orchestration.
Thinking: This is a specific AI reasoning strategy where the model plans internally without external feedback during the planning phase, relying on its learned world model. It's about the AI's internal cognitive process for planning.

Problem: Adapting plans dynamically in response to intermediate execution results and environmental feedback, especially in complex and dynamic environments.
Context: A foundation model needs to solve complex tasks where decisions at each step depend on preceding context and outcomes. The environment is 'visible' to the controller, allowing for closed-loop interaction.
Solution: Generate plans incrementally, one step at a time, by iteratively interacting with the environment and utilizing feedback (from the environment and/or human) obtained from previous executions. This allows the controller to reason about the current context and generate alternative or refined plans.
Result: More rational and adaptable planning, better suited for complex tasks like multi-step QA and embodied learning. Enables models to handle exceptions appropriately and develop more refined subsequent plans.
Related Patterns: Self-Ask, ReAct, ToolFormer, Inner Monologue, LLMPlanner.
Uses: Interactive tasks, embodied learning, multi-step question answering, scenarios requiring dynamic adaptation and error handling.
Thinking: This pattern describes an AI-specific reasoning strategy that emphasizes continuous interaction with the environment and feedback loops, a core concept in intelligent agents and adaptive AI systems.

Problem: Training foundation models to use tools effectively by mimicking the behavior of human experts or other capable models.
Context: A foundation model needs to acquire tool-use skills, and expert demonstrations (human-annotated or model-generated) are available, often in the form of state-action pairs or complete trajectories.
Solution: Optimize the model's parameters using imitation learning, typically behavior cloning. This involves training the model in a supervised fashion to imitate expert actions given certain inputs or conditions, assuming the expert's behavior is optimal or near-optimal.
Result: Models learn to imitate human experts' actions, significantly improving both in-domain performance and out-of-distribution generalization for tool-oriented tasks.
Related Patterns: Supervised Learning for Tool Use, Semi-supervised Learning for Tool Use, Self-supervised Learning for Tool Use, Behavior Cloning.
Uses: Initial training of AI agents for tool use, especially when expert data is available or can be generated, to bootstrap learning.
Thinking: This pattern describes a fundamental AI learning paradigm (imitation learning) applied to the specific domain of tool use, focusing on how AI acquires skills by observing others.

Problem: Training foundation models to utilize tools without requiring extensive human behavior annotation or seed-labeled datasets, which are time-consuming and labor-intensive.
Context: A foundation model needs to learn tool use with minimal human effort, leveraging its own inherent capabilities and a small number of initial examples.
Solution: Leverage the in-context learning ability of foundation models to iteratively bootstrap tool-use examples based on a handful of human-written examples. These auto-generated examples are then filtered to reduce noise, creating a self-supervised dataset.
Result: Significantly improves tool-use performance by generating sufficient supervision in a self-supervised manner, highlighting the potential of self-supervised learning for enhancing tool-use capabilities with reduced human intervention.
Related Patterns: Toolformer, In-context Learning, Few-shot Learning.
Uses: Rapidly enabling foundation models to learn new tools with very few initial examples, reducing the data annotation burden.
Thinking: This pattern describes a cutting-edge AI learning paradigm (self-supervised learning, specifically leveraging in-context learning) applied to the problem of tool acquisition, showcasing AI's ability to generate its own training data.

Pattern Name: Learning from Feedback (Reinforcement Learning for Tool Use)
Problem: Enabling artificial agents (foundation models) to learn better tool-use behaviors through trial and error, adapting to changes and optimizing decisions based on dynamic feedback.
Context: Tool learning can be considered a complex decision-making process where the action space is defined by tools, and the agent needs to learn to select appropriate tools and perform correct actions to maximize a reward signal.
Solution: Frame tool learning as a Reinforcement Learning (RL) scenario. A foundation model is initialized as the policy model, leveraging its prior knowledge. A reward function quantifies the agent's performance. The agent learns to reflect on the current state, select tools, and perform actions that lead to the highest expected reward.
Result: Agents learn better behaviors through trial and error, adapting to changes and optimizing decisions based on dynamic feedback. This adaptability is crucial for developing LLMs that can effectively handle a variety of tools and environments, enhancing their practical utility and robustness.
Related Patterns: Environment Feedback for Tool Learning, Human Feedback for Tool Learning (RLHF), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).
Uses: Developing adaptable and robust AI agents for tool use, especially in dynamic, interactive environments where optimal strategies are not known beforehand.
Thinking: This pattern applies a core AI learning paradigm (Reinforcement Learning) to the problem of tool use, emphasizing adaptive behavior and learning from consequences, which is fundamental to intelligent agents.

Problem: Aligning AI models' tool-use behavior with human preferences, values, and nuanced requirements, which are often difficult to define with programmatic rewards.
Context: AI models need to learn subjective or complex aspects of tool use, safety, and trustworthiness that require human judgment to guide their behavior.
Solution: Humans provide rewards and penalties (explicit or implicit) based on the model's generated plans or actions. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is then employed to finetune a reward model to imitate human preferences, which subsequently optimizes the policy with RL algorithms (e.g., PPO).
Result: Models learn to align with human preferences, improving their ability to manipulate tools in ways that are helpful, harmless, and trustworthy, even for complex, long-form tasks, and can surpass performance of models trained solely on supervised demonstrations.
Related Patterns: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), InstructGPT, WebGPT.
Uses: Fine-tuning AI agents for tool use where human alignment, safety, trustworthiness, and subjective quality are critical, such as in conversational agents or high-stakes scenarios.
Thinking: This pattern describes a crucial AI alignment technique (RLHF) applied to guide tool-using agents, addressing ethical, safety, and preference-based challenges unique to advanced AI systems.

Problem: Enabling foundation models to transfer learned tool-use skills to new tools and situations efficiently, given the massive and rapidly expanding array of tools, without requiring extensive re-training for each new tool.
Context: Models need to learn to use a wide variety of tools efficiently and adapt to novel scenarios. Collecting enough supervised tool-use data for every tool is time-consuming and practically infeasible.
Solution: Recognize commonalities and patterns of tools to synthesize and transfer knowledge and skills. This is achieved through: 1) **Interface Unification:** Designing a unified interface (semantic, GUI, or programming) for consistent tool manipulation. 2) **Meta Tool Learning:** Training models to learn optimal tool-use strategies that can be transferred. 3) **Curriculum Tool Learning:** Gradually introducing models to increasing tool complexity.
Result: Models can synthesize and transfer knowledge and skills more easily and efficiently, adapting to new tools and scenarios, reducing the need for extensive supervised data and enabling more adaptable and intelligent ML models.
Related Patterns: Interface Unification, Meta Tool Learning, Curriculum Tool Learning, Transfer Learning, Multitask Learning.
Uses: Developing highly adaptable and scalable AI agents capable of using a broad and evolving set of tools, minimizing the effort required for new tool integration.
Thinking: This pattern addresses a core AI challenge: generalization and transfer learning, specifically in the context of tool use. It focuses on how AI can learn to apply skills broadly rather than just memorizing specific tool interactions.

Pattern Name: AI Tool Creation (From User to Maker)
Problem: Expanding the capabilities of AI beyond merely using existing tools to autonomously creating new tools or encapsulating existing ones, challenging traditional views of human-exclusive tool creation.
Context: Foundation models demonstrate strong code generation capabilities and a deep understanding of tool functionalities, suggesting a potential for them to contribute to the tool lifecycle.
Solution: Leverage large code models to generate executable programs (which can be deemed as new tools) based on language descriptions. Foundation models can also encapsulate existing APIs into more advanced functions, extending their utility. This involves designing tools specifically for AI (modularity, AI-friendly formats) and enabling AI to generate tools.
Result: AI systems can autonomously develop sophisticated solutions, transitioning from passive tool users to active tool makers. This implies the potential for foundation models to contribute to the evolution of tools themselves.
Related Patterns: Code Generation, Model-as-Programmer.
Uses: Automating software development, creating specialized AI-optimized tools, enhancing existing tool functionalities, and exploring the creative potential of AI.
Thinking: This pattern describes an evolutionary role for AI, moving from consumption to creation of tools. It's a significant leap in AI capabilities, demonstrating AI's potential to innovate and contribute to its own ecosystem, which is a unique AI design concept.

Problem: Foundation models, typically trained on generic domains, struggle to process personal information and provide tailored assistance to users with varying needs and preferences for tool learning.
Context: Users have heterogeneous preferences, language styles, and personal information (e.g., historical conversation records, social networks) that should influence how an AI agent manipulates tools.
Solution: 1) **Aligning User Preference with Tool Manipulation:** Model heterogeneous user information into a unified semantic space and develop personalized tool execution plans and tool calls based on individual user preferences. 2) **From Reactive to Proactive Systems:** Shift from models only responding to queries to initiating actions on behalf of the user, continually improving performance based on user interaction history. 3) **Privacy Preserving Technologies:** Develop secure and trustworthy mechanisms to access and process user data while protecting user privacy.
Result: Models provide more personalized and precise responses, adapt to diverse user expressions, and potentially act proactively, while addressing critical privacy concerns inherent in handling personal data.
Related Patterns: User-centric Natural Language Generation, Proactive Systems, Privacy-Preserving AI.
Uses: Any AI assistant or agent that needs to adapt its tool-use behavior to individual users, providing tailored experiences in domains like email, online shopping, or scheduling.
Thinking: This pattern addresses the AI challenge of personalization and user-centric design in tool interaction, including ethical and privacy considerations unique to AI systems handling personal data.

Problem: Discrepancies inevitably arise between different knowledge sources (model's internal knowledge, augmented knowledge from tools, or knowledge from different tools), leading to inaccurate or unreliable model predictions.
Context: Foundation models are augmented with external tools (e.g., text retrievers, calculators, Python interpreters) to enhance their generation with domain-specific or up-to-date knowledge. These sources may contain outdated, false, or biased information.
Solution: 1) **Conflict Detection:** Models should first detect potential conflicts among different sources and flag them for further investigation. 2) **Conflict Resolution:** Models need to make verification, choose reliable sources, and provide explanations for their generation by interpreting which knowledge source is considered and how it is augmented into the final response.
Result: Models can correct their own beliefs, discern knowledge conflicts, and integrate tool responses correctly and reliably, improving factual accuracy, trustworthiness, and explainability in model predictions.
Related Patterns: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), Explainable AI, Trustworthy AI.
Uses: Any AI system that combines internal knowledge with external tool-provided information, especially in high-stakes scenarios like medical assistance, legal advice, or financial transactions where accuracy and reliability are paramount.
Thinking: This pattern addresses a critical AI challenge when integrating external knowledge: managing inconsistencies and ensuring trustworthiness. It's about the AI's ability to critically evaluate and synthesize information from multiple, potentially conflicting, sources.

Problem: Real-life tasks are usually complicated and multi-step, bringing severe hardness for LLM agents in planning through a one-step process.
Context: LLM-based agents need to accomplish complex, multi-step tasks in varied and complex environments.
Solution: Adopt the 'divide and conquer' idea by decomposing a complicated task into several simpler subtasks and then sequentially planning for each subtask. This can be 'decomposition-first' (decompose all subtasks then plan) or 'interleaved' (dynamically decompose and plan based on feedback).
Result: Significantly enhances the ability of LLM agents to solve complicated tasks. Decomposition-first methods create stronger correlations between subtasks and original tasks, reducing task forgetting and hallucinations. Interleaved methods dynamically adjust decomposition based on environmental feedback, improving fault tolerance.
Related Patterns: Chain-of-Thought (CoT), ReAct, HuggingGPT, Plan-and-Solve, ProgPrompt, PAL, Program-of-Thought (PoT), Visual ChatGPT.
Uses: Multimodal tasks, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, symbolic reasoning, robot task planning, general reasoning and planning, image processing.
Thinking: This pattern directly addresses a core challenge in AI planning: breaking down complex problems into manageable sub-problems. Its application to LLMs, leveraging their reasoning capabilities for subtask generation and planning, makes it a specific AI design pattern for LLM agents.

Problem: Due to the complexity of tasks and the inherent uncertainty of LLMs, a single plan generated by an LLM is likely to be suboptimal or even infeasible.
Context: LLM agents need to generate robust and optimal plans for complex tasks where a single generative output might be insufficient or unreliable.
Solution: Lead the LLM to think more by generating various alternative plans for a task (multiplan generation). Then, employ a task-related search algorithm to select the optimal plan to execute. Multiplan generation often uses sampling strategies or explicit prompting, while selection uses heuristic search algorithms (e.g., majority vote, BFS, DFS, MCTS, A*).
Result: Provides a broader exploration of potential solutions in the expansive search space, leading to more robust and potentially optimal plans. Improves reasoning and problem-solving capabilities.
Related Patterns: Self-consistency, Tree-of-Thought (ToT), Graph-of-Thought (GoT), LLMMCTS, RAP, LLM-A*.
Uses: Improving chain-of-thought reasoning, deliberate problem-solving, large-scale task planning, robotics, general plan generation and evaluation.
Thinking: This pattern leverages classic AI search and decision-making techniques (like tree search, MCTS, A*) to overcome the inherent stochasticity and potential suboptimality of LLM outputs. It's an AI pattern for improving the quality and reliability of LLM-generated plans.

Problem: LLMs face challenges when confronted with environments featuring intricate constraints (e.g., mathematical problems, generating admissible actions) and may struggle with efficiency or feasibility, especially for less common constraints.
Context: LLM agents need to generate plans that strictly adhere to complex constraints or require high efficiency, which LLMs alone might not reliably achieve due to their statistical nature.
Solution: Integrate LLMs with external, specialized planners (either symbolic or neural). The LLM primarily plays a supportive role, such as formalizing tasks into a planner-compatible language (e.g., PDDL) or providing high-level reasoning, while the external planner handles the constrained planning or efficient execution.
Result: Elevates the planning procedure by addressing issues of efficiency and infeasibility of generated plans. Leverages the theoretical completeness, stability, and interpretability of symbolic systems, or the superior planning efficiency of neural planners within specific domains. Accelerates the construction of symbolic models.
Related Patterns: LLMP, LLMDP, LLMPDDL, LLMASP (symbolic); CALM, SwiftSage (neural).
Uses: Mathematical problem-solving, generating admissible actions, dynamic interactive environments, model-based task planning, text-based games, complex interactive tasks.
Thinking: This is a hybrid AI pattern that combines the strengths of LLMs (natural language understanding, task formalization) with specialized AI planning systems (symbolic AI for rigorous constraint satisfaction, neural AI for domain-specific efficiency). It's a clear AI design pattern for leveraging different AI paradigms.

Problem: LLM agents may make errors, get stuck in thought loops, or suffer from hallucinations during planning due to limited feedback and insufficient reasoning abilities for complex problems.
Context: LLM agents need to improve their fault tolerance and error correction capabilities during the planning process, especially in complex or interactive environments.
Solution: Encourage the LLM to reflect on failures, suboptimal outcomes, or environmental feedback, and then iteratively refine the plan. This often involves a process of plan generation, feedback (self-generated or from external tools/evaluators), and subsequent refinement based on that feedback.
Result: Enhances fault tolerance and error correction capabilities, helps agents correct errors, break out of thought loops, and significantly reduces factual errors. Improves performance on complex tasks.
Related Patterns: Self-refine, Reflexion, CRITIC, InteRecAgent, LEMA.
Uses: General plan generation and refinement, interactive recommendation agents, improving reasoning in LLMs, self-correction with tool-interactive critiquing, learning from mistakes.
Thinking: This pattern directly implements a cognitive AI mechanism: learning from mistakes and iterative self-improvement. It's about enabling the AI agent to evaluate its own performance and adjust its strategy, which is a fundamental aspect of intelligent behavior.

Problem: LLMs have limited context windows and struggle with retaining fine-grained details or leveraging long-term knowledge, which hinders their planning capabilities, especially for long-running or knowledge-intensive tasks.
Context: LLM agents need to access and utilize valuable information (e.g., commonsense knowledge, past experiences, domain-specific knowledge) beyond their immediate context window to enhance planning and growth.
Solution: Enhance planning with an extra memory module where valuable information is stored and retrieved when needed, serving as auxiliary signals. This can be achieved through RAG-based methods (external storage and retrieval) or Embodied Memory (finetuning LLM parameters with experiential samples).
Result: Demonstrates enhanced growth and fault tolerance in planning by providing access to long-term knowledge and experiences. RAG-based methods offer real-time, low-cost updates, while finetuning provides larger memorization capacity.
Related Patterns: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), Generative Agents, MemoryBank, TiM, RecMind, MemGPT, REMEMBER (RAG-based); CALM, TDT, AgentTuning (Embodied Memory).
Uses: Enhancing LLMs with the latest knowledge, storing and retrieving daily experiences, long-term memory for LLMs, text-based games, generalized agent abilities, semi-parametric reinforcement learning.
Thinking: This pattern addresses a fundamental limitation of LLMs (context window, knowledge retention) by integrating external or embedded memory mechanisms. It's a classic AI approach to knowledge representation and utilization for intelligent agents, adapted for LLMs to improve their planning over time and across contexts.

Pattern Name: Few-Shot LLM Planning for Embodied Agents
Problem: Existing methods for embodied agents require a large number of labeled examples (language instructions and gold trajectories) to learn each task, leading to high data costs and poor sample efficiency, which hinders the development of versatile agents capable of many tasks and quick learning of new tasks.
Context: Building versatile embodied agents (e.g., robots) that can follow natural language commands to complete complex tasks and learn new tasks quickly in visually-perceived, partially-observable environments.
Solution: Harness the power of Large Language Models (LLMs) as a high-level planner. LLMs are prompted with natural language instructions and a small number of exemplar pairs of instruction-high-level plan (HLP) in their context (in-context learning/few-shot setting) to directly generate high-level plans (sequences of subgoals). This approach avoids the need for extensive task-specific training data or parameter updates.
Result: Achieves competitive performance with significantly less training data (e.g., less than 0.5% of paired training data) compared to baselines trained using full datasets. This enables the development of versatile and sample-efficient embodied agents that can quickly learn many tasks.
Related Patterns: Hierarchical Planning (LLM-based High-Level, Dedicated Low-Level), In-Context Learning, Dynamic In-Context Example Retrieval, Logit Biases for Constrained Generation, Grounded Replanning.
Uses: LLMPlanner, SayCan (though SayCan uses LLM for ranking, LLMPlanner uses it for direct generation).
Thinking: This pattern describes a core AI problem (data efficiency for embodied agents) and an AI-specific solution (leveraging LLMs' few-shot learning capabilities for planning). It's a central theme of the research.

Problem: Complex, long-horizon tasks for embodied agents are difficult to solve end-to-end. Directly generating primitive actions from natural language instructions is challenging and prone to errors, especially in diverse environments.
Context: Embodied agents operating in diverse, partially-observable environments, needing to follow natural language instructions for complex tasks that involve multiple steps and interactions.
Solution: Adopt a hierarchical planning model that separates high-level reasoning from low-level execution. An LLM serves as the high-level planner, generating a sequence of abstract subgoals (e.g., 'Navigation potato', 'Pickup potato'). A separate, often pre-trained or synthetically trained, low-level planner then maps each subgoal into a sequence of primitive actions executable in the current environment and state. This makes low-level planning conditionally independent of the natural language instruction.
Result: Simplifies the overall planning problem by decoupling high-level strategic reasoning from low-level tactical execution. Improves effectiveness in complex vision-and-language navigation (VLN) or embodied instruction following tasks, particularly in low-data regimes, by allowing specialized modules for each level of abstraction.
Related Patterns: Few-Shot LLM Planning for Embodied Agents, Grounded Replanning.
Uses: LLMPlanner, HLSM, FILM, SL3.
Thinking: This is an architectural pattern for AI systems, specifically for embodied agents. It defines how an LLM is integrated into a multi-level control system, leveraging its strengths for abstract planning while delegating concrete action generation to a specialized component. The text explicitly describes this structure.

Problem: High-level plans generated by LLMs, while plausible, often lack physical grounding to the current environment, leading to unattainable plans, incorrect object references, or an inability to adapt to unforeseen environmental changes or execution failures. Static plans cannot adjust to dynamic real-world conditions.
Context: Embodied agents executing LLM-generated high-level plans in dynamic, partially-observable environments where initial plans might become invalid, suboptimal, or encounter unexpected obstacles or object locations.
Solution: Implement a dynamic replanning algorithm. When the agent encounters an issue during execution (e.g., fails to execute an action, takes too long to reach a subgoal), the LLM is re-prompted. The prompt is augmented with a list of objects currently perceived in the environment (physical grounding). The LLM then generates a new, more grounded continuation of the partial high-level plan. Logit biases can further prioritize observed objects in the LLM's output.
Result: Enables LLMs to dynamically adapt generated high-level plans to the current environment, overcoming unattainable plans and improving task completion success rates. Creates a closed-loop feedback mechanism between the environment and the LLM, making the agent more robust and adaptable to real-world complexities.
Related Patterns: Few-Shot LLM Planning for Embodied Agents, Hierarchical Planning (LLM-based High-Level, Dedicated Low-Level), Logit Biases for Constrained Generation.
Uses: LLMPlanner.
Thinking: This pattern describes a specific AI control mechanism for making LLM-based planning robust and adaptive in dynamic environments. It directly addresses the 'grounding problem' in AI by incorporating real-time environmental feedback into the planning loop.

Problem: The performance of LLMs in in-context learning is highly sensitive to the choice of in-context examples. Randomly selected examples may not be relevant or informative for a given test task, leading to suboptimal performance.
Context: Using LLMs for few-shot learning where a small set of training examples is available, and the goal is to maximize performance for diverse test tasks by providing the most relevant demonstrations.
Solution: For each test example, dynamically retrieve the most similar examples from the small set of paired training examples. This is typically achieved using a k-nearest neighbor (kNN) retriever, which calculates similarity (e.g., Euclidean distance) between embeddings (e.g., BERT embeddings) of the instructions for the test example and all available training examples.
Result: Significantly improves in-context learning performance by providing more relevant and informative demonstrations to the LLM, leading to better quality outputs and higher task success rates.
Related Patterns: Few-Shot LLM Planning for Embodied Agents, In-Context Learning.
Uses: LLMPlanner, also mentioned in related work (30, 32, 9, 20).
Thinking: This is a specific technique to optimize the *AI learning process* (in-context learning for LLMs). It's not a general software pattern but directly impacts the AI model's ability to learn from examples effectively.

Problem: When using LLMs for generative tasks like planning, the output needs to be constrained to a predefined set of allowed actions and objects. Without such constraints, the LLM might generate invalid or irrelevant tokens, or struggle to disambiguate references to objects in the environment.
Context: Using LLMs to generate structured outputs (e.g., high-level plans) for embodied agents, where the actions are finite and objects are specific entities in the environment. The LLM's output needs to adhere to these domain-specific constraints and potentially prioritize observed entities.
Solution: Apply logit biases during LLM generation. This involves adjusting the probabilities (logits) of specific tokens in the LLM's output layer. For instance, bias logits to favor allowed high-level actions and objects defined in the environment, or to prioritize objects currently observed in the environment (e.g., from an object detector).
Result: Constrains the LLM's output to valid actions and objects, making the generated plans more executable and grounded. Improves robustness by guiding the LLM to correctly interpret ambiguous instructions (e.g., 'lamp' to 'TableLamp') or map natural language references to environment-specific object names (e.g., 'RecycleBin' to 'GarbageCan').
Related Patterns: Grounded Replanning, Few-Shot LLM Planning for Embodied Agents.
Uses: LLMPlanner.
Thinking: This is a technique directly applied to the *output generation mechanism of an LLM* to improve its adherence to task-specific constraints and environmental grounding. It's an AI-specific control mechanism that influences the model's probabilistic output.

Problem: Large pretrained language models (LMs) struggle with knowledge-intensive NLP tasks due to limited ability to access and precisely manipulate factual knowledge, difficulty in providing provenance, challenges in updating world knowledge, and a tendency to hallucinate.
Context: Knowledge-intensive NLP tasks requiring language generation (e.g., question answering, fact verification, creative generation) where models need to produce factual, specific, and diverse outputs, and where external, updatable knowledge is crucial.
Solution: Combine a pretrained parametric memory (a seq2seq model like BART) with a nonparametric memory (a dense vector index of a knowledge source like Wikipedia accessed by a pretrained neural retriever like DPR). The retriever provides relevant documents (latent variables) conditioned on the input, and the generator then conditions on these retrieved documents along with the input to generate the output. The entire system (retriever and generator) is fine-tuned end-to-end by marginalizing over the latent documents.
Result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on open-domain QA tasks, generates more specific, diverse, and factual language compared to parametric-only baselines, and allows for easy updating of world knowledge by replacing the nonparametric memory.
Related Patterns: Hybrid Parametric-Nonparametric Memory, RAGSequence Model, RAGToken Model, REALM, ORQA, Memory Networks, Retrieve-and-Edit approaches.
Uses: Open-domain Question Answering, Abstractive Question Answering, Jeopardy Question Generation, Fact Verification, and other knowledge-intensive NLP generation tasks.
Thinking: This is the central pattern described in the paper. It defines a novel architectural approach for combining two distinct AI components (a generator and a retriever) and a specific training methodology (end-to-end fine-tuning with latent variable marginalization) to solve a core AI problem (knowledge limitations in LMs).

Problem: How to effectively integrate retrieved documents into a sequence-to-sequence generation process when a consistent context from a single document is desired for the entire output sequence.
Context: Within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework, when generating a target sequence where the entire sequence is likely to be coherent with or derived from a single retrieved passage, or when computational efficiency for decoding is a concern for per-token retrieval.
Solution: Treat the retrieved document as a single latent variable that is marginalized to get the seq2seq probability. The model retrieves the top-K documents, and for each document, the generator produces the probability of the complete output sequence. These probabilities are then marginalized (summed) across the top-K documents. The same retrieved document is used to predict each target token in the sequence.
Result: Achieves strong performance on various knowledge-intensive tasks, particularly effective when a single, coherent document provides sufficient context for the entire generated output. Generates more diverse outputs than RAGToken in some cases.
Related Patterns: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), RAGToken Model (alternative marginalization strategy).
Uses: Open-domain Question Answering, Abstractive Question Answering, Fact Verification.
Thinking: This is a specific strategy within the broader RAG pattern, detailing a particular way to handle the latent document variable during generation. It's an AI design choice for how to condition a generative model on retrieved information.

Problem: How to effectively integrate retrieved documents into a sequence-to-sequence generation process when different parts of the output sequence might benefit from different retrieved documents, allowing for more dynamic context switching.
Context: Within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework, when generating a target sequence where different tokens or segments of the output might draw information from distinct retrieved passages, requiring a more flexible conditioning mechanism.
Solution: Allow the model to draw a different latent document for each target token and marginalize accordingly. The top-K documents are retrieved, and for each output token, the generator produces a distribution for that token given each document. These per-document token probabilities are then marginalized (summed) before selecting the next token, and the process repeats for the subsequent token.
Result: Performs well, especially noted for tasks like Jeopardy Question Generation where combining content from several documents is beneficial. Offers flexibility in drawing information from multiple sources during generation.
Related Patterns: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), RAGSequence Model (alternative marginalization strategy).
Uses: Open-domain Question Answering, Jeopardy Question Generation, Fact Verification.
Thinking: Similar to RAGSequence, this is another specific strategy within RAG, focusing on per-token conditioning on retrieved documents. It's an AI design choice for dynamic context integration in generative models.

Problem: Purely parametric language models (LMs) struggle with limitations such as difficulty in expanding or revising their knowledge, inability to provide provenance for predictions, and a tendency to 'hallucinate' (generate factually incorrect information).
Context: AI systems, particularly large language models, operating in knowledge-intensive domains where factual accuracy, updatability, and interpretability of knowledge are critical requirements.
Solution: Design an AI system that combines a parametric memory (knowledge stored in the model's weights, e.g., a pretrained seq2seq transformer) with an explicit, retrieval-based nonparametric memory (e.g., a dense vector index of a large text corpus like Wikipedia). The parametric component handles general language understanding and generation, while the nonparametric component provides access to specific, verifiable, and updatable factual knowledge.
Result: Overcomes limitations of parametric-only models by enabling direct revision and expansion of knowledge, allowing inspection and interpretation of accessed knowledge, reducing hallucinations, and improving factual accuracy and specificity of generated text.
Related Patterns: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), REALM, ORQA, Memory Networks, Stack-augmented networks, Memory layers.
Uses: General knowledge-intensive NLP tasks, Open-domain Question Answering, Fact Verification, Language Generation, Dialogue Systems.
Thinking: This pattern describes a fundamental architectural principle for AI systems that need to manage and leverage knowledge effectively. RAG is a concrete instantiation of this broader pattern. It addresses a core AI challenge of knowledge representation and utilization.

Problem: Updating the world knowledge of parametric-only AI models is costly and time-consuming, as it typically requires extensive retraining of the entire model when new information becomes available or existing information changes.
Context: AI systems that rely on external knowledge sources and need to remain current with rapidly evolving real-world information (e.g., current events, dynamic databases).
Solution: Design the AI system such that its nonparametric memory component (e.g., a document index used by a retriever) can be replaced or updated independently at test time without requiring retraining of the parametric components (e.g., the generator or query encoder). This involves separating the explicit knowledge base from the learned model parameters.
Result: Enables dynamic and efficient updating of the model's world knowledge, allowing it to adapt to new information quickly and cost-effectively without incurring the high computational expense of full model retraining. Improves accuracy for tasks requiring up-to-date information.
Related Patterns: Hybrid Parametric-Nonparametric Memory (this pattern is a key advantage and design implication of using such a hybrid architecture).
Uses: Any knowledge-intensive AI application where the underlying factual knowledge changes frequently, such as real-time question answering, news summarization, or systems interacting with dynamic databases.
Thinking: This pattern highlights a specific design advantage and capability of certain AI architectures, particularly those employing nonparametric memory. It's an AI system design pattern focused on knowledge lifecycle management and adaptability.

Problem: Lack of a unified framework to organize existing language agents and plan future developments, leading to custom terminology and difficulty in comparison and building new agents with clean abstractions.
Context: Designing and developing language agents that augment Large Language Models (LLMs) with external resources or internal control flows for tasks requiring grounding or reasoning.
Solution: Propose a conceptual framework that organizes language agents along three key dimensions: 1) their information storage (divided into working and long-term memories), 2) their action space (divided into internal and external actions), and 3) their decision-making procedure (structured as an interactive loop with planning and execution).
Result: Provides a blueprint to structure language agents, allowing for retrospective survey and organization of existing work, and prospective identification of underexplored directions towards more capable agents. It contextualizes modern language agents within the broader history of AI.
Related Patterns: Structured Memory Modules, Structured Action Space, Deliberative Decision-Making Cycle, LLM as Probabilistic Production System.
